extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics instructors, mathematics education researchers, and practitioners interested in inquiry-based instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for designing, enacting, researching, and assessing inquiry-based (IBL/IOI) instruction in undergraduate mathematics courses, emphasizing classroom practices, curricular design, instructor moves, equity, and research agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students engage deeply with coherent and meaningful mathematical tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Students engage deeply with coherent and meaningful mathematical tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquiry curricula exhibit a longer-term trajectory that sequences daily tasks to build toward big ideas; these coherent task sequences scaffold students’ mathematical work on challenging problems over weeks of instruction and may lead to proving a major theorem or (re)inventing a mathematical idea, definition, or procedure. Instructors should choose important mathematical ideas and develop tasks that enable students to meet and grapple with them; a good task sequence helps provide the framework. Avoid treating active learning as a collection of one-off activities that do not build toward larger disciplinary goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students collaboratively process mathematical ideas
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students talk to each other about what they are doing and thinking; conversations clarify, solidify, and elaborate learners’ ideas and build communication and collaborative skills. Observable practices include small-group problem solving, students presenting and sharing tentative work, whole-class discussions for critique and sense-making. Instructors should structure opportunities for students to reflect, analyze, synthesize, and communicate and ensure students have equal chances to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructors inquire into student thinking
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors elicit student ideas, make those ideas public, interpret and use student thinking to move the mathematical agenda forward, and connect students’ ideas to formal/conventional mathematics. This requires listening, adaptive and responsive facilitation, and deep mathematical knowledge. Examples of talk moves: “Tell us how you thought about it…”, “Did anyone think about that in a different way?”, and “What do the rest of you think about what Jason just said?” Instructor talk is not absent but is well timed and well targeted to surface and explore students’ prior knowledge and to support changing views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructors foster equity in their design and facilitation choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors foster equity in their design and facilitation choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable instructional practice is a core pillar of IBME: instructors must notice whose thoughts are heard, acknowledged, and valued, actively shape participation patterns, and use equity-oriented practices (e.g., assigning competence, structuring participation) to include all in rigorous mathematical learning and identity-building. Research shows inquiry classrooms can promote equity but it is not automatic—intentional strategies, instructor reflection, and attention to classroom dynamics are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent learning trajectories / sequenced task design
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiry curricula should exhibit coherent learning trajectories and sequenced task design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instructional sequences that scaffold students’ progress toward big ideas; draw on learning-trajectory research (learning-trajectory based instruction, LTBI) to coordinate research on teaching with research on learning. Curriculum design should consider how tasks reveal and build students' intermediate understandings and how daily tasks connect across weeks to support long-term development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students reinvent or create mathematics and engage in disciplinary practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Students reinvent or create mathematics that is new to them by engaging in mathematical practices similar to those of practicing mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students do conjecturing and proving, defining, creating and using algorithms, modeling, and other authentic disciplinary practices. Instructors allow intellectual space for creativity while extending and connecting student ideas to formal mathematics, fostering ownership and deep understanding rather than mere procedural fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and sociomathematical norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Classrooms should establish social norms (students share thinking; students orient to and engage in others’ thinking) and sociomathematical norms (criteria for mathematical acceptability, difference, and elegance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote norms where students routinely explain reasoning, listen and make sense of others’ thinking, offer different solution strategies, and justify agreement/disagreement with reasons. Use norms to make explicit what counts as acceptable or elegant mathematical work; these norms guide classroom discourse and are teachable targets for instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor practices: helping students deepen thinking and building on student ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should help students deepen their thinking and build on and extend student ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond promoting sharing and engagement, effective instructors use concrete facilitation moves to deepen reasoning (e.g., probing questions, revoicing, pressing for justification) and to leverage student contributions to advance the collective mathematical agenda. Research (Rasmussen et al., 2018) provides actionable talk moves to realize these goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully designed, sequenced, and classroom-tested instructional materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use carefully designed, sequenced, and classroom-tested instructional materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IO curricula in particular rely on materials grounded in design heuristics and classroom-based research; materials should be tested and iterated in situ (design-based research). While IBL materials are often practitioner-developed and shared collegially, both traditions benefit from materials that are sequenced, scaffolded, and informed by observed student learning. Avoid ad hoc or untested problem sets that lack coherent sequencing toward disciplinary goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic Mathematics Education (RME) design heuristics / bottom-up curriculum design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design curricula bottom-up using RME heuristics so learners can reinvent important mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than presenting expert knowledge as fixed truths, use tasks and contexts that support learners' progressive reinvention of concepts and procedures. Use design-based research cycles (design-implement-analyze) to reveal productive routines and teacher knowledge needed to support reinvention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit teaching and assessment of transferable skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly teach and assess transferable skills such as communication, teamwork, writing, metacognition, and ethical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although inquiry classrooms afford opportunities for these skills, instructors should call them out, design tasks and assessments targeting them, and help students reflect on their broader gains. Doing so also helps justify IBME pedagogies to colleagues and meet accreditation or program learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable indicators of IBME in the classroom
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete observable features that indicate IBME enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visitors to IBME/IO/IBL classrooms would see students working in small groups on unfamiliar and challenging problems, students presenting tentative work, whole-class discussions that question and refine reasoning, instructor mini-lectures used for closure/signposting, and instructor roles focused on guiding, managing, coaching, and monitoring rather than solely telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity-focused instructor moves (e.g., assigning competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use equity-focused instructor moves such as assigning competence to publicly raise the status of students’ intellectual contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices that explicitly support inclusion—calling on and valuing diverse contributions, structuring participation, and fostering norms of respect and responsibility—are necessary complements to inquiry practices. Instructors must consider students’ feelings and identity-work in addition to cognitive tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research design and measurement choices for studying IBME
rubrics_metrics.description: Select appropriate research designs and outcome measures when studying IBL/IOI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IBL studies have often used aggregate, multi-course measures (grades, surveys, interviews) suitable for heterogeneous samples; IO studies have used course-specific content assessments and detailed classroom discourse analyses in design-based research contexts. Researchers should align measures to research questions (e.g., course-specific learning vs. generalizable transferable skills) and design studies with sufficient power to examine equity/intersectional outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop instructor knowledge and supports for implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide professional development, collegial networks, and supports to help instructors adopt and adapt inquiry approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communities of practice, workshops, SIGMAA, course repositories, and videotaped exemplars can support instructor learning. Implementation requires attention to department/organizational features and ongoing support (peer observation, reflective practice, online networks). Avoid expecting instructors to adopt IBME without targeted supports.
